title: When Mount St. Helens Blew Its Top
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Dave sitting in for Jerry) explain the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens in Washington. They cover how stratovolcanoes form in the Cascade arc, the mountain's long eruptive history and Native American legends (LeWitt), its naming after Baron St. Helens, the March 1980 earthquake swarm and growing bulge, USGS volcanologist David Johnston's warnings, the evacuation fight and Harry Truman who stayed, the May 18, 1980 lateral blast triggered by a north-flank landslide, the Dorothy Stoffel flyover, the pyroclastic blast, lahars, ash fallout, ecological recovery, aftereffects on Spirit Lake, the 2004 to 2008 activity, and a listener mail segment about old Scottish dialect terms.

segments.title: Opening banter and volcano background
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about butter and their excitement for the Mount St. Helens topic, then discuss how the mountain's TV coverage and scientists' attention shaped the story.

segments.title: How stratovolcanoes form
segments.summary: The hosts explain stratovolcanoes forming from subduction in the Cascade arc, magma backing up beneath a sealed crust, and the bulge that grew about six feet a day.

segments.title: Native legends, naming, and prior eruptions
segments.summary: The mountain's Indigenous name LeWitt and its legend are discussed, along with naming after Alan Fitz Herbert, an ancient eruption about 4,000 years ago with thick ash fallout, and 19th-century eruptions documented by Paul Kane.

segments.title: Forest setting and March 1980 earthquakes
segments.summary: The area's National Forest status and recreation at Spirit Lake are described, followed by the March 1980 magnitude 4.0 earthquake and swarm that drew geologists to the mountain.

segments.title: Warnings, evacuation, and Harry Truman
segments.summary: David Johnston and Don Swanson of the USGS push for evacuation and a red zone against pressure from the logging company Weyerhaeuser and recreation groups. Harry Truman, who refused to leave his lodge with his cats, becomes a folk figure. Smaller eruptions in March and April build toward May.

segments.title: Reopening and the morning of May 18
segments.summary: After activity calmed, residents were allowed back under waivers and a porous perimeter, contributing to a death toll of 57. Johnston stayed at Cold Water II while colleagues were sent away, and the mountain blew at 8:32 am on May 18, 1980.

segments.title: Lateral blast and north flank collapse
segments.summary: The hosts explain why the eruption was a lateral blast rather than from the summit: superheated water under the north-side bulge flashed to steam once the earthquake triggered the largest recorded landslide. Dorothy Stoffel's flyover account is quoted.

segments.title: Blast zone, lahars, and victims
segments.summary: The blast traveled north at high speed with extreme heat, destroying everything within about eight miles. David Johnston and Jerry Martin, the ham radio operator, died. Lahars and flooding followed, and huge rock debris moved down valleys.

segments.title: Aftereffects, ash, ecology, and later eruptions
segments.summary: Spirit Lake rose and became shallower, the summit lowered, ash affected crops and power, animals in the blast zone died while ecosystems recovered, the plume circled the globe, survivors' escapes were described, and the 2004 to 2008 activity and research station were noted.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the episode with a closing remark and sign-off.
